text_and_author: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica, Book 4 (3rd century BC); Pseudo-Apollodorus, Bibliotheca (1st-2nd century AD); Ruvo krater (c. 400 BC).
passage_reference: Ap. Rhod. Arg. 4.1638-1688 (Talos episode, spell 4.1665-1672 [uncertain: exact lines], ankle wound 1679-1680, fall 1685-1688); Apollodorus, Bibl. 1.9.26; Plato, Minos 320c (Talos and the laws).
greek_term_and_translation: Apollonius: Keres (death-spirits), Hades' hounds, Medea's 'evil eye' and 'phantoms/visions' sent on his mind; ichor 'like molten lead'. Translators: Race (Loeb), Green, Seaton, Hunter. Exact Greek words for the evil-eye and phantom images not verified here. [uncertain] 'Robot', 'ichor as power' and 'perception attack' are modern glosses.
maker_or_origin: Apollonius: last of the bronze race, born from ash trees. Apollodorus: Hephaestus's gift to Minos, or son of Kres. Sources disagree.
what_it_does: Guards Crete, circles the island (three times a year in Plato's Minos, carrying the laws) and throws rocks at ships.
what_it_lacks: No mind or choice is stated. He is unable to see through the trick, which is the point: he is fooled through his senses.
failure_mode: Deception and vulnerability, not a hardware fault. Medea bewitches his sight or mind and he wounds his ankle on a rock, so the ichor drains. In Apollodorus one version has Medea drive him mad with drugs; another has her promise immortality and pull the nail. This matches AI failures where the system is fooled by crafted input and has a single point of failure.
tradition_variance: Apollonius: spell and evil eye, then the ankle scrape. Apollodorus: Medea's drugs and madness; or Poeas shoots him in the ankle; or the nail is pulled. Plato does not describe his death. So there is no one canonical death.
who_is_the_judge: Medea decides and acts. Minos owns the guardian but does not intervene. Talos judges nothing. The Argonauts, not the guardian, are the ones deliberating.
origin_of_intelligence: None stated for Talos. He is not shown thinking. Medea's spell works on his perception, which implies that he sees, but the text does not say he understands.
how_it_is_used: Mayor reads Talos as an ancient artificial being and the ankle nail as a design flaw. Some 2025-26 AI commentators use the spell as an early case of adversarial input. [uncertain: specific commentators]
reception_accuracy: partial. Apollonius does have a spell on the senses, but he also gives the ankle wound and ichor, which readers merge into one 'hack'. 'Adversarial attack' is a modern gloss.
angle_fit: supports. The guardian enforces but has no judgement, and it is beaten by a mind (Medea) that fools it. That is a failure of perception with no stated deliberation.
counter_argument_strength: A sceptic can say a spell is magic, not a cognitive failure, and that Talos's death is variously a nail, an arrow or drugs, so 'death by perception' is only one strand. The essay should name Apollonius specifically and say other authors differ.
claim_status: Apollonius's text is ancient fact. 'Death by perception' as a category is scholarly-adjacent interpretation. Mapping it to AI failure is modern gloss.
quotable_line: Apollonius 4.1679-80: ichor flowed 'like molten lead' from the ankle (Race/Green wording, check before quoting). [uncertain]
essay_paragraph_fact: In Apollonius, Talos does not fail mechanically. Medea, from the Argo, casts her eye and sends visions on him, and he grazes his single vulnerable ankle on a rock, so his ichor runs out. A guardian with no judgement is beaten by a mind that can fool it.
honest_caveat: Sources disagree on how Talos dies (spell, drugs, arrow, nail). Greek terms for the evil eye and visions need checking against the Greek text and a named translation before quoting.
